title: Brace for Impact
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Marking his 95th Substack post, Victorian teacher Shaun Brien reflects on a career that began in a culture where every teacher was expected to build bespoke resources from scratch and keep them private. He recalls being told on a Monday to teach a unit the next day, and admits he was selfish with his materials early on because senior-years competition made him think his work was for his class alone. His view has reversed: teachers have a responsibility to have an impact beyond their own four walls, and expertise that leaves with a teacher is lost to the profession. He tells how lockdown lesson videos shared on YouTube ended up used by Victorian schools years later, and credits the Substack community of teacher-writers for showing that his ideas had value. His call to action is to use your voice, develop thick skin, and recognise that even people who left the classroom can still help many teachers, followed by a list of 16 Australian education writers to read.
points: Teacher expertise too often sits with individuals and disappears when they move on, which is why shared, consistent resources matter.
Withholding resources for the sake of a competitive edge limits the benefit of hard work, and Brien now thinks teachers should have impact beyond their own classes.
A lesson video recorded for lockdown students became a free resource used by schools across the state, showing how unexpected a ripple can be.
Writing publicly built his confidence to have professional conversations with school leaders when something does not sit right.
The post closes with a list of 16 Australian education Substacks, but its substance is the argument to use your voice.
quotes: When I started my career as a teacher there was this reverence and expectation for the individual teacher to create bespoke resources for their classes from scratch.

On my first teaching placement I remember being told on a Monday that I would be teaching on Tuesday morning and that the class was currently up to this specific point in the topic and therefore I needed to go home and prepare the rest of the unit.

So much of teacher knowledge and expertise seems to be tied specifically to individuals. A large majority of those individuals will teach in one school for most of their life, doing the important work day in and day out but when they move on, that expertise moves on with them.

In my opinion now it is our responsibility as teachers to have the widest impact we can. This does not mean that every teacher needs to be attempting to benefit education on a macro level but I do think it is important that a teachers impact is felt wider than just the class which they teach.

It was only when I got feedback from a student that they found the videos helpful because they could both use closed captioning and rewind and rewatch specific examples when they got stuck that I had the idea of uploading the lessons to YouTube and sharing them with wider teaching networks.
In all honesty though, if you have a voice, use it. Whether it be on a school level, a network level or a system level. If you see or hear a problem, call it out.
The amazing part of the process of writing here and developing my voice is that it has also helped to develop thicker skin.
So if you can have an impact, or have thoughts about education, use your voice, you never know who it might affect.
